newsitem.title: POLAND: Suspected arson damages Warsaw's only synagogue.
newsitem.headline: Suspected arson damages Warsaw's only synagogue.

text.p: An apparent arson attack after midnight on Wednesday devastated part of Warsaw's only synagogue, arousing shock in a city most of whose Jewish population was murdered by German invaders in World War Two.
"I have seen synagogues go up in flames before...such events reopen wounds which had begun to heal a little," Poland's Chief Rabbi Menachem Joskowicz told a news conference.
Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski said it was an act of barbarism and vowed that such actions would be prosecuted with the full force of the law.
The blaze wrecked the building's disused old main entrance and left a large vestibule charred and littered with debris.
Jewish community leaders invited Warsaw citizens of good will to gather at the synagogue during the evening service to show solidarity. Radio stations broadcast the appeal.
"Our initial conclusions show the cause was probably arson," Warsaw police press officer Tomasz Grzelewski said.
"It had to be some inflammable substance thrown in through a window over the entrance," he told Reuters, adding that it was too early to reveal theories about who was responsible.

The fire at the central Warsaw Nozyk synagogue was spotted by an employee of a Jewish charity sleeping in a nearby building and by a policeman posted outside the Jewish theatre on a city square some metres away, who both summoned help.
One person sleeping in apartments adjoining the synagogue was treated for smoke poisoning, Rabbi Michael Schudrich and other Jewish community leaders said in a statement.
Only quick action by the fire brigade stopped the flames from engulfing the building's main prayer hall, they said.

They said that two days before the fire an anonymous telephone caller to the Ronald S. Lauder Foundation, a Jewish educational charity represented by Schudrich, had threatened "a bomb has been planted or will be planted very soon."

Most of Poland's pre-1939 Jewish population of more than three million were murdered by the German Nazis -- many in the hellish Getto the invaders created, then levelled, in an area only a few blocks from where the Nozyk synagogue stands.

Many thousands of survivors later emigrated in waves, in part prompted by anti-Semitic episodes such as a 1946 pogrom in the city of Kielce and an "anti-Zionist" campaign launched by a faction of the then ruling communist party in 1968.

While there are some tiny extremist groups hostile to minorities, all mainstream Polish parties condemn anti-Semitism and democratic governments since the 1989 fall of communism have sought to improve ties with Jews and Israel.
"Poles want to build good, friendly relations with Jews in Poland and around the world. Criminal behaviour by individuals cannot disrupt this," Kwasniewski said in his statement.

He said the attack went against Poland's traditions of tolerance and said it was especially painful to the Poles as it was aimed against a community that had lived in the country for 800 years and fallen victim to Nazi genocide.
But some figures on the fringes of right-leaning parties have made remarks insulting to Jews in recent years -- notably Henryk Jankowski, a priest linked with the Solidarity union.
Jewish leaders said a failure by these parties and society to condemn such remarks strongly enough might create an atmosphere in which anti-Semitic attacks would be more likely.
"They (remarks) are met with deafening silence," Konstanty Gebert, editor of a Jewish monthly, said outside the synagogue.
A bomb last year smashed windows of Warsaw's kosher restaurant, also near the synagogue, but the motive or exact target of the attack have not so far been explained.
Schudrich called on police to step up patrols of the area around the synagogue, housing key sites of Warsaw Jewish life.
